If the survey is repeated with a random sample of $294$ members and the results are calculated in the same way, which of the following will be the most likely effect of using the larger random sample compared to the smaller random sample?

options.content: The margin of error will be lower.
The margin of error will be higher.
The estimate of the percentage of the gym's members that would continue to pay for a membership if the price increased will be lower.
The estimate of the percentage of the gym's members that would continue to pay for a membership if the price increased will be higher.

article: A district school board in a certain state is proposing a change to the length of lunch periods for all high schools in the district. A sample of 365 high school students was selected at random from all high school students in the district. The selected students were asked whether they approved of the proposed change, and 211 students responded that they did not approve.
stem:
A district school board in a certain state is proposing a change to the length
of lunch periods for all high schools in the district. A sample of 365 high
school students was selected at random from all high school students in the
district. The selected students were asked whether they approved of the
proposed change, and 211 students responded that they did not approve.
Which of the following is the largest population to which the results of the
survey can be generalized?

options.content: All high school students in the district
All high school students in the state
The 211 students who responded that they did not approve of the proposed change

article: A company that produces only one type of item wants to estimate the percent of the items produced in a typical week that are defective. A random sample of 540 of the items produced in a certain week were tested. Based on the sample, it is estimated that 12.5% of all items produced by the company in this week are defective, with an associated margin of error of 2.79%. Based on the estimate and associated margin of error, which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion about all items produced by the company during this week?

options.content: It is plausible that between 9.71% and 15.29% of the items are defective.

article: A town manager selected 2 random samples of residents in the town to estimate the percentage of all residents that planned to vote in favor of a new business in the downtown area. Based on the first sample, he estimated that 75% of the residents in the town planned to vote in favor, with an associated margin of error of 8.5%. Based on the second sample, he estimated that 83% of the residents in the town planned to vote in favor, with an associated margin of error of 6.9%. Assuming the margins of error were calculated the same way, which of the following best explains why the first sample obtained a larger margin of error than the second sample?
stem: A town manager selected $2$ random samples of residents in the town to estimate the percentage of all residents that planned to vote in favor of a new business in the downtown area. Based on the first sample, he estimated that $75$% of the residents in the town planned to vote in favor, with an associated margin of error of $8.5$%. Based on the second sample, he estimated that $83.6$% of the residents in the town planned to vote in favor, with an associated margin of error of $6.9$%. Assuming the margins of error were calculated the same way, which of the following best explains why the first sample obtained a larger margin of error than the second sample?

options.content: The first sample contained more residents than the second sample.
The first sample contained fewer residents than the second sample.
The first sample contained a higher percentage of residents that planned to vote in favor of a new business in the downtown area.
The first sample contained a lower percentage of residents that planned to vote in favor of a new business in the downtown area.

article: For a study, a group of chipmunks will be selected from a habitat consisting of 220 chipmunks, and a group of prairie dogs will be selected from a habitat consisting of 190 prairie dogs. Some of the chipmunks and prairie dogs will be in a treatment group, and some of the chipmunks and prairie dogs will be in a control group.
stem:
For a study, a group of chipmunks will be selected from a habitat consisting of $220$ chipmunks, and a group of prairie dogs will be selected from a habitat consisting of $190$
prairie dogs. Some of the chipmunks and prairie dogs will be in a treatment group, and some of the chipmunks and prairie dogs will be in a control group. Which of the following is necessary for this study to attempt to establish a cause-and-effect relationship betweentwo variables?

options.content: The number of chipmunks in the treatment group is equal to the number of prairie dogs in the treatment group, and the number of chipmunks in the control group is equal to the number of prairie dogs in the control group.
The chipmunks and the prairie dogs are randomly assigned to the treatment and control groups.
The chipmunks and the prairie dogs are randomly selected from their respective habitats.

The average age of the chipmunks in the treatment group is equal to the average age of the prairie dogs in the treatment group, and the average age of the chipmunks in the control group is equal to the average age of the prairie dogs in the control group.

stem: A machine fills bags with approximately $11$ ounces of sugar. To test the accuracy of the filling process, $132$ bags of sugar were selected at random and weighed. Based on the sample, it is estimated that the average weight of all bags of sugar filled by the machine in an $8$-hour period is $10.83$ ounces, with an associated margin of error of $0.2$ ounce. Which of the following is the best interpretation of this estimate?

options.content: Plausible values for the average weight of all bags of sugar filled by the machine are between $10.63$ ounces and $11.03$ ounces.
Plausible values for the average weight of all bags of sugar filled by the machine are less than $10.63$ ounces or greater than $11.03$ ounces.
The average weight of all bags of sugar filled by the machine is greater than $10.98$ ounces.
The average weight of all bags of sugar filled by the machine is less than $10.98$ ounces.

stem: A survey was conducted in Madison to estimate the percent of adult residents who support the addition of streetlights at every corner in their town. Based on the survey, it is estimated that $40\%$ of all adult residents of Madison support the addition of streetlights at every corner in their town, with an associated margin of error of $6\%$. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion about all adult residents of Madison?

options.content: Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Madison who support the addition of streetlights at every corner in their town are between $34\%$ and $46\%$.
The addition of streetlights at every corner in the town is supported by exactly $34\%$ of all adult residents of Madison.
Plausible values for the percent of all adult residents of Madison who support the addition of streetlights at every corner in their town are either less than $34\%$ or more than $46\%$.
The addition of streetlights at every corner in the town is supported by more than $46\%$ of all adult residents of Madison.

stem: An inspector checked a sample of 370 scales selected at random from a population of 8,000 scales to estimate what percentage of the 8,000 scales were inaccurate. From this sample, the inspector estimated that 9% of the 8,000 scales were inaccurate, with an associated margin of error of 2.9%. Which of the following is the most appropriate conclusion?

options.content: It is plausible that between 488 and 952 of the scales in the population are inaccurate.
It is plausible that fewer than 488 of the scales in the population are inaccurate.
Exactly 720 of the scales in the population are inaccurate.
It is plausible that more than 952 of the scales in the population are inaccurate.

stem: A sample consisted of 750 people selected at random from all adult residents in a certain city. Based on the sample, the estimated percentage of all adult residents who think taxes are too high was 62%, with an associated margin of error of 3.47%. Which of the following best describes the range of plausible values for the percentage of all adult residents in the city who think taxes are too high.

options.content: Any value greater than 58.53% and less than 65.47%
Any value less than 58.53% or greater than 65.47%

options.content: The margin of error is between 4.37% and 5.37%.
The margin of error is less than 2.37%.

The margin of error is greater than 5.37%.

article: In a survey of smartphone owners, 64% of a random sample of younger adults aged 18-29 used their phones to listen to music or podcasts, compared to 21% of a random sample of older users who did so. Based on the results of this survey, which of the following conclusions are valid?
stem:
In a survey of smartphone owners, $64\%$ of a random sample of younger adults aged $18$-$29$ used their phones to listen to music or podcasts, compared to $21\%$ of a random sample of older users who did so. Based on the results of this survey, which of the following conclusions are valid? $$$$

$\text{I}$ : Younger adults are more likely to listen to music or podcasts on their smartphones than are older adults. $$$$
$\text{II}$ : Older adults like music less than younger adults. $$$$
$\text{III}$ : Older adults do not listen to music on their smartphones because they find it inconvenient. $$$$
$\text{IV}$ : Younger adults are more likely than older adults to own smartphones.

In a blind taste test of the onions, tasters indicated that the onion grown in soil with lower sulfur content was sweeter. Based on the information provided, which of the following is a reasonable conclusion?

article: In 2016, a polling agency surveyed 5,000 US adults with full-time employment who were selected at random and asked each of them, 'Are you satisfied with the benefits provided by your employer?' Of those surveyed, 68 percent responded they were satisfied with the benefits provided by their employers. Based on the results of the survey, which of the following are reasonable conclusions?
stem:
In $2016$, a polling agency surveyed $5{,}000$ US adults with full-time employment who were selected at random and asked each of the them, "Are you satisfied with the benefits provided by your employer?" Of those surveyed, $68$ percent responded they were satisfied with the benefits provided by their employers. Based on the results of the survey, which of the following are reasonable conclusions? $$$$

$\text{I}$. About $68$ percent of all US adults are satisfied with the benefits provided by their employers. $$$$
$\text{II}$. About $68$ percent of all US adults with full-time employment are satisfied with the benefits provided by their employers. $$$$
$\text{III}$. About $68\%$ of full-time employees at any US company are satisfied with the benefits provided by their employers.

article: In a 2021 online poll with 15,000 responses from US adults, 61 percent of US adults responded that they think they can win an unarmed fight against a goose. Based on the results of the poll, which of the following statements must be true?
stem:
In a $2021$ online poll with $15{,}000$ responses from US adults, $61$ percent of US adults responded that they think they can win an unarmed fight against a goose. Based on the results of the poll, which of the following statements must be true? $$$$
$\text{I}$. About $61$ percent of US adults have won unarmed fights against geese. $$$$
$\text{II}$. About $61$ percent of the world adult population think they can win an unarmed fight against a goose. $$$$
$\text{III}$. lf $15{,}000$ randomly selected US adults were surveyed, about $61$ percent of them would respond that they think they can win an unarmed fight against a goose.

article: Near the end of a US cable news show, the host invited viewers to respond to a poll on the show’s website that asked, “Do you support the new federal policy discussed during the show?” At the end of the show, the host reported that 28% responded “Yes,” and 70% responded “No.”

article: To determine the mean number of children per household in a community, Tabitha surveyed 20 families at a playground. For the 20 families surveyed, the mean number of children per household was 2.4.

options.content: The mean number of children per household in the community is $2.4$.

The sampling method is flawed and may produce a biased estimate of the mean number of children per household in the community.
The sampling method is not flawed and is likely to produce an unbiased estimate of the mean number of children per household in the community.
